summary: This program builds a list of five Book objects, then collects their genres into a HashSet so each genre appears only once, and prints the resulting set. It shows the difference between a List, which keeps every value you add, and a Set, which silently drops duplicates.

lines.text: Set is the interface for a collection that holds no duplicate elements; declaring variables with this type keeps the code independent of which set implementation you choose.
HashSet is the concrete class being used here, and it is the fastest general-purpose Set when you do not care about ordering.
The books themselves still live in a List, because the library needs to keep every book even when two share a genre.

lines.code: Book hobbit = new Book("The Hobbit", "J.R.R. Tolkien", "Fantasy");
lines.text: Three of the five books use the genre "Fantasy", which is exactly the duplication the Set is meant to collapse.
The set is declared as Set<String> but created as a HashSet, a common Java habit of programming to the interface rather than the implementation.
The enhanced for loop visits each Book in turn so the program can inspect its genre.
Adding a genre that is already in the set does nothing, so "Fantasy" is stored once no matter how many fantasy books exist.
A HashSet has no defined order, so the genres may print in any sequence — use a TreeSet when order matters.
